topic: Why savings grow slowly, then fast

opening.say: Say you put some money in a savings account that pays interest. Most people expect the balance to climb in a nice straight line.
But it doesn't. The balance after t years follows a rule where the time sits up in the exponent, and that changes everything.
So let's watch what that rule actually draws, and pay attention to how steep it is early on compared with later.

more.say: Here's a quick example. Start with one hundred dollars at seven percent. After one year you earn seven dollars of interest.
The next year, you earn interest on one hundred seven dollars, not one hundred. So that year's interest is a little bigger than the last.
Each year the pile of money earning interest is larger, so each year's gain is larger too. Gains start feeding on themselves.

plan.setup: Watch the curve and how its steepness changes.
plan.narration: [[curve-appears]]Early on, the curve looks almost flat. Each year's interest is small because the balance is small. [[later-gains]]But the balance keeps growing, so each year earns more than the last. [[steepening]]Interest starts earning its own interest, and the climb gets steeper and steeper. [[doubling]]That's why the late years feel so dramatic.
plan.plan:
curve-appears: the curve B of t equals one hundred times one point zero seven to the t draws from t equals zero, starting at one hundred, nearly flat.
later-gains: two small bars mark the dollar gain in an early year and a later year, the later bar clearly taller.
steepening: a tangent line slides along B, getting visibly steeper; its slope equals the yearly gain rate, which grows with B.
doubling: markers show the balance reaching two hundred near ten years, then four hundred near twenty, equal time steps, bigger jumps.
plan.close: If you added to the account each year, would the curve bend sooner?
